front: Name the three mechanical valve types and describe flow through each.
back: 1) Ball-and-cage (Starr-Edwards) — flow around the cage, high peak velocities, central closing regurgitant jet. 2) Single tilting-disc — two orifices (major and minor). 3) Bileaflet tilting-disc (St Jude, On-X) — three orifices with three physiologic 'washing' regurgitant jets.

front: What is a Ross procedure and what long-term complication is characteristic?
back: Ross procedure = autograft replacement of the aortic valve using the patient's own pulmonary valve (a pulmonary homograft is placed in the pulmonary position). Late complication: autograft aortic regurgitation.

front: How deep from the annulus are balloon-expandable (Sapien) and self-expanding (CoreValve/Evolut) TAVR valves typically deployed?
back: Sapien: 2–4 mm below the annulus. CoreValve/Evolut: 3–6 mm below the annulus.

front: What is the recommended post-operative TTE follow-up schedule for bioprosthetic vs mechanical valves?
back: Both: initial TTE 2–4 weeks postoperatively to establish baseline. Bioprosthetic: annual TTE after 10 years. Mechanical: only if a change in symptoms or exam.

front: What is a normal peak velocity across an aortic prosthesis?
back: Less than 3 m/s. Velocities > 4 m/s or discordant DVI/AT suggest obstruction or PPM.

front: Define the Doppler velocity index (DVI) for aortic and mitral prostheses.
back: Aortic: V_LVOT / V_jet (or VTI_LVOT / VTI_jet). Mitral: V_jet / V_LVOT. Aortic normal DVI ≥ 0.35; < 0.25 suggests obstruction. Mitral VTI ratio > 2.2 abnormal.

front: Why is the DVI preferred over gradient alone for aortic prosthesis evaluation?
back: It is FLOW-independent and PROSTHESIS-SIZE independent — corrects for high output, PPM, small prostheses that would otherwise inflate gradient readings.

front: What acceleration time cutoff on the aortic prosthesis CW jet suggests pathologic obstruction?
back: AT > 100 ms suggests pathologic obstruction. Also: AT/ET > 0.4 indicates obstruction.

front: Contrast the CW jet contour of a normal vs pathologically obstructed aortic prosthesis.
back: Normal (or high-flow, PPM, pressure recovery): triangular/pointed early-peaking jet. Pathologic obstruction: rounded, mid-systolic (parabolic) peak.

front: Define iEOA and the thresholds for aortic patient-prosthesis mismatch.
back: iEOA = EOA / BSA. Aortic PPM present: iEOA < 0.85 cm²/m². Severe PPM: iEOA < 0.65 cm²/m². (Mitral PPM: < 1.2 moderate; < 0.9 severe.)

front: Why does patient-prosthesis mismatch develop and why is it not a valve malfunction?
back: PPM occurs when a normal, structurally intact prosthesis has an EOA too small for the patient's cardiac output demand (small valve in a large body). It reflects a size mismatch, not a mechanical valve problem.

front: What is the single most important Doppler finding for pathologic obstruction of a mitral prosthesis?
back: PHT ≥ 130 ms. This single value is the strongest indicator of pathologic mitral prosthesis obstruction.

front: E velocity ≥ 1.9 m/s and VTI ratio ≥ 2.2 on a mitral prosthesis with a NORMAL PHT (< 130 ms) — most likely diagnosis?
back: Significant mitral prosthesis REGURGITATION. Elevated flow raises E and VTI ratio, but PHT remains short because there is no true obstruction to LV filling.

front: Which equation should be used to calculate mitral prosthesis EOA — continuity or PHT?
back: Continuity equation: EOA = (CSA_LVOT × VTI_LVOT) / VTI_prosthesis. PHT-derived MVA overestimates prosthesis EOA and should NOT be used.

front: When is the continuity equation invalid for prosthesis EOA?
back: When significant AR or MR is present — LVOT-derived flow no longer equals valve flow.

front: Are microcavitations seen with mechanical valves pathologic?
back: No — microcavitations (microbubbles) are commonly seen with NORMALLY functioning bileaflet mechanical valves, especially on harmonic imaging.

front: Distinguish paravalvular from central prosthetic regurgitation.
back: Central: originates within the prosthesis. Small central 'washing' jets are normal for mechanical valves; larger central jets suggest bioprosthetic degeneration or endocarditis. Paravalvular: originates outside the sewing ring — ALWAYS pathologic.

front: Compare echocardiographic features of prosthetic valve thrombus vs pannus.
back: Thrombus: acute onset symptoms, larger, soft (similar echogenicity to myocardium), more common in mechanical mitral, mobile — may respond to anticoagulation. Pannus: gradual chronic symptoms, small, dense/echogenic, more common in aortic position, fixed — requires surgery.

front: Prosthetic aortic valve endocarditis with vegetation or root abscess most commonly causes what hemodynamic complication?
back: Aortic regurgitation. Less commonly AV block or acute MI from coronary compromise.

front: In which scenario is prosthetic-valve pressure recovery most clinically significant?
back: Small mechanical bileaflet aortic prostheses in patients with a small ascending aorta. Doppler overestimates gradient (and underestimates EOA) relative to catheter measurements.

front: What degree of prosthetic mitral valve 'rocking' motion suggests dehiscence?
back: Rocking motion > 15° across the annulus (best assessed by 3D echo). This is the gold-standard imaging finding for prosthetic MV dehiscence.

front: How do you handle a mechanical mitral prosthesis with a 'double spectral' Doppler profile?
back: Use the BRIGHTER (higher-velocity) portion of the profile for gradient calculation — this represents true transvalvular flow. The lower-velocity signal is central/orifice-related.

front: Age criteria that generally favor a BIOPROSTHESIS vs a MECHANICAL valve?
back: Bioprosthesis favored: age > 70 (low structural deterioration risk, avoid long-term anticoagulation). Mechanical favored: age < 50 (bioprosthesis has 15-y structural failure ~30% at age 40, 50% at age 20).

front: Which additional patient factors favor a bioprosthetic vs mechanical valve?
back: Bioprosthesis: high bleeding risk on anticoagulation, limited access to INR monitoring, non-compliance, small aortic root (allows future valve-in-valve TAVR). Mechanical: existing indication for anticoagulation (AF), high reoperation risk, compliant with INR.

front: What is the aortic regurgitation index (post-TAVR) and its cutoff for poor prognosis?
back: ARI = (Diastolic BP − LV end-diastolic pressure) / SBP × 100. ARI < 25 is associated with worse post-TAVR outcomes (measured invasively in the cath lab).

front: State two prosthetic valve findings that always warrant urgent evaluation.
back: Paravalvular regurgitation (always pathologic), and new hemolytic anemia with schistocytes/helmet cells (suggests high-shear paravalvular leak).
